newsitem.title: CHINA: Enron to drill 3 wells in new China block.
newsitem.headline: Enron to drill 3 wells in new China block.

text.p: Enron Oil & Gas Co said it will drill three new wells and redevelop three existing ones over the next two years in its new block in China's southwestern province of Sichuan.
The company will spend around $5 million on the initial two-year development phase, company officials said on Tuesday.

Development could begin in 1999 with eventual marketable natural gas reserves in the multi-trillion cubic feet equivalent range, they said, but added it was too soon to make detailed output predictions.

Enron on Monday signed a 30-year production sharing contract with the China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) to develop oil and gas reserves in a 728,000 hectare (1.8 million acre) block in the southwestern province of Sichuan.

Conditions in the Sichuan block meant extraction would be far from easy, but success could be a major boost for Enron in what the U.S. firm hoped would be a long-term involvement in China, Enron Oil & Gas chairman Forrest Hoglund said.
"Our hopes are that, if we can demonstrate very strong results, then this (project) will be very beneficial," Hoglund told a news briefing in Beijing.
"We view China as a very, very attractive place in which to invest," he said.

Enron, which holds a 100 percent interest in the block, would apply its experience extracting oil and gas from "tight sand" -- or highly impervious -- reservoirs in Texas and the Rocky Mountains to deal with similar conditions in the Sichuan basin, Hoglund said.
"This is a challenging reservoir," he said, adding that one advantage of working in Sichuan, one of China's oldest oil-producing areas, was the existence of a ready market for natural gas.

Sichuan already has an extensive gas pipeline network with existing spare capacity of around 70 million cubic feer per day (mmcfd), while unsatisfied demand was estimated at around 40-50 mmcfd, he said.
"It's one more positive thing about this venture: that we are not worried about the market," Hoglund said.

China has worked hard to boost oil and gas exploration and exploitation in recent years as energy demand surges along with economic growth. Oil imports are soaring as domestic fields are unable to keep up with the new demand.
Beijing was becoming ever more welcoming of foreign investment, Hoglund said.
He declined to give details of the Sichuan contract's terms for revenue sharing but said they were well within the usual range for international deals.

While Chinese companies had drilled wells into the Sichuan block's shallow oil reserves, its deeper gas zones had been basically undeveloped, said Dennis Ulak, president of Enron Oil & Gas International Inc.
